_about: 'The history behind this' notes (press H). Say plainly what is sourced and what is invented. Sources are listed in docs/research.md.
history.place.grahamstown: Grahamstown was founded as a military post in 1812. The 1820 Settlers made it the centre of the Albany district and of the frontier trade in hides, ivory and tallow. In April 1837 the English settlers here gave a large Dutch Bible to Piet Uys's departing party.
history.place.cradock: Cradock, on the Great Fish River, was one of the frontier towns trekkers passed on their way north.
history.place.colesberg: Colesberg was at the north-eastern edge of the Cape Colony. In 1839 the traveller James Backhouse found meal very dear there: 75 shillings a muid, while some farmers kept their old price of 6 to 10 rixdollars.
history.place.orange_colesberg: The trekkers called the Orange River the Groot Rivier (Great River). Parties crossed it at several drifts. The western road in this game crosses near Colesberg.
history.place.philippolis: Philippolis was a Griqua town north of the Orange River, founded around a mission. The Griqua were a people of mixed Khoikhoi and colonial descent with their own leaders. In January 1837 Griqua riders were allies of the trekkers at Mosega.
history.place.tarka: The Tarka district, under the Winterberg, was frontier farming country hit hard in the war of 1834-35. Many trek families came from districts like this.
history.place.stormberg: The Stormberg mountains lie on the eastern road north. That the mountain road here was cold and snowy in winter is a reasonable guess, not yet checked against a source.
history.place.buffelsvlei: Piet Retief's party crossed the Orange at Buffelsvlei in March 1837. The town of Aliwal North was later built there.
history.place.caledon_drift: The Caledon River ran between trekker routes and the lands of Moshoeshoe's Basotho to the east.
history.place.thaba_nchu: In 1833 the Barolong under their leaders, with Wesleyan missionaries led by James Archbell, moved from Platberg on the Vaal to Thaba Nchu. After the battle of Vegkop in October 1836, Moroka sent oxen to bring the stranded trekkers to Thaba Nchu.
history.place.vet_river: The Vet River runs across the Highveld north of Thaba Nchu. The trekker settlement of Winburg grew up near here.
history.place.sand_river: In 1837 the trekker parties gathered in a united laager by the Sand River. The Uys party is said to have reached it on 29 June 1837, though one study says the Uys party joined the others at Thaba Nchu in August.
history.place.vaal_drift: North of the Vaal lay country Mzilikazi's Ndebele had held since the early 1830s. After Vegkop and Mosega in 1836-37, the Ndebele moved north, out of reach of the trekker commandos.
history.place.mooi_river: Hendrik Potgieter's people settled on the Mooi River, where Potchefstroom was founded in December 1838 or June 1839 (sources disagree). Barolong and Bahurutshe communities lived here before the trekkers.
history.river.orange: Rivers were among the most dangerous parts of a trek. Crossing the Orange in 1836, Captain Harris had to build raised platforms inside his wagons to keep his goods dry. Some parties floated their wagons over, and others waited for the water to drop.
history.river.caledon: The Caledon River formed part of the western edge of the Basotho lands.
history.river.vet: The Vet River is a Highveld river, low in winter.
history.river.vaal: The Vaal River was called the Likwa by the Batswana.
history.grahamstown_bible: This scene is history: in April 1837 the 1820 Settlers of Grahamstown, led by Thomas Philipps and W.R. Thompson, presented a large Dutch Bible to Piet Uys's departing trek. The Bible is now at the Voortrekker Monument. Your family's part in the scene is invented.
history.colesberg_edge: The Cape of Good Hope Punishment Act (1836) let colonial courts try British subjects for crimes committed in the lands beyond the Colony. Britain did not stop the trekkers at the border, but it claimed they were still British subjects.
history.buffelsvlei: Retief's party crossed the Orange at Buffelsvlei in March 1837. The people your family meets here are invented.
history.thaba_nchu: Moroka's help after Vegkop is history: he sent oxen to bring Potgieter's stranded people to Thaba Nchu. The Barolong had their own interests and alliances in these years; they were not simply helpers in the trekkers' story.
history.sand_river: In 1837 the trekker parties gathered in a united laager by the Sand River and argued over leaders and where to go next. English families among the trekkers were rare, so an English family would have had to earn trust. Your family's welcome is invented.
history.vaal_news: In January 1837 a trekker commando, with Barolong and Griqua allies, attacked the Ndebele town of Mosega and took about 6,000 cattle. American missionaries living at Mosega left with the commando. The herder's account in this scene is invented, to give the Ndebele side of events.
history.mooi_river: Families like yours settled along the Mooi River from 1838. For the Barolong and Bahurutshe who lived there, the trekkers' arrival was the start of a long struggle over the land.
history.karoo_water: This event is invented, adapted from an early design idea. Dysentery (the flux) was a danger on many journeys, but there is no good count of how many trekkers it killed.
history.oxen_stray: This is history: in June 1839 James Backhouse's party near Colesberg was held up when the oxen strayed after smelling grass far away.
history.horses_go_home: This is history: on his 1836 journey Captain Harris lost two horses in the night, and his men thought they had gone back to where they were bred.
history.wagon_hole: This is history: near Graham's Town in 1836, Captain Harris's baggage wagon turned over in a deep hole by the road and the upper works were smashed.
history.quicksand: This is history: crossing the Little Fish River in 1836, Captain Harris's horse sank in a quicksand and nearly drowned.
history.mirage: This is history: in the dry country north of the Orange, Harris's thirsty oxen ran for a shining 'lake' that was only salt crust on the ground.
history.dogs_paws: This is history: Harris's dogs had their paws burned raw by the hot ground. They were treated with the tar-and-fat mixture used to grease the axles, and afterwards held out a paw to ask for more.
history.church_town: This is history: the frontier towns grew round their churches. Graham's Town had a Wesleyan chapel from 1822 and the Anglican church of St George from 1830. Cradock's Dutch Reformed congregation dates from 1818 and its first church from 1824; Colesberg's congregation from 1826, and its church's foundation stone was laid in 1830. For trekkers and settlers alike, Sunday worship and rest mattered greatly.
history.church_mission: This is history: Wesleyan missionaries came to Thaba Nchu with Moroka's Barolong in 1833. The mission was a meeting place for the Barolong, the missionaries and the trekkers who passed through.
history.church_laager: This is history: Erasmus Smit, a former missionary, was ordained as minister to the trekkers on 21 May 1837. There were no churches on the road, so the trekkers held their services in the laagers, under awnings or in a tent, and many kept the Sabbath on the road. The first trekker church north of the Orange was built at Kerkspruit in October 1837.
history.hyenas: This is history: hyenas drawn by the smell of mutton came into Harris's camp at night and took what was left out.
history.storm_cattle: This is history: in a storm, the sound of reeds thrashing frightened Harris's cattle so much that 'they thrice broke loose'.
history.quagga: This is history: in June 1839 Backhouse saw 'a troop of Quaggas, with their foals' near Colesberg. The quagga, a kind of zebra striped only at the front, was hunted to extinction. The last wild ones died in the late 1870s and the last in a zoo in 1883.
history.lions: Lions were common on the Highveld in the 1830s, and travellers' accounts describe them attacking cattle at night. This event is invented.
history.servant_wages: Wages here are from period sources: a cattle leader or wagon driver earned about 10 rixdollars (15 shillings) a month around 1832-1838. From 1828, Khoikhoi in the Colony no longer had to carry passes, so they could leave an employer who treated them badly. African workers did not have the same freedom. Slavery at the Cape ended in law on 1 December 1834, but the freed people stayed bound to their former owners as unpaid 'apprentices' until 1 December 1838.
history.smous: Smouse were travelling traders who took goods to farms far from any town, often taking sheep in payment. The smous you meet is invented.
history.snakebite: This event is invented. Travellers on the frontier described the rinkhals, a spitting cobra.
history.frost: Highveld winters have hard frosts at night. This event is invented.
history.griqua: Griqua riders, mounted and armed, were a strong force around the Orange River. This meeting is invented.
history.barolong: Among the Batswana, including the Barolong, beads were the usual medium of exchange in the 1830s, according to Captain Harris. Tobacco had lost value because people now grew it themselves.
history.vegkop: At Vegkop in October 1836, Potgieter's laager of wagons held off a large Ndebele force. Two trekkers were killed, and many of the attackers. Potgieter lost 5,000 sheep, 300 cattle and 100 draught oxen. The family you meet is invented.
history.retief_manifesto: Piet Retief's manifesto, printed in the Graham's Town Journal in early 1837, listed the trekkers' complaints: losses in the frontier wars, labour laws, the loss of enslaved workers when slavery ended, and British rule. Historians still argue over which of these mattered most.
history.governors_man: Very few English settlers went north with the trekkers. An English family would have met suspicion. This scene is invented.
history.stuck_wagon: This event is invented. It gives an English family a way to earn the trekkers' trust.
history.frontier_war_prices: Captain Harris wrote in 1836 that the recent war had 'trebled the price of every thing, and of live stock in particular'. In December 1838, James Backhouse still paid 45 rixdollars an ox near Grahamstown, a price 'considered high in this country'.
history.vegkop_prices: After Vegkop, Potgieter's people had lost most of their cattle, so oxen were scarce among the trekkers in early 1837. The size of this price rise is a guess.
history.colesberg_grain: In June 1839 meal at Colesberg cost 75 shillings a muid, against an 'old price' of 6 to 10 rixdollars (9 to 15 shillings). The cause is not recorded. The shopkeeper blames the trekkers, which fits the time but is not proven.
